All parties have fought space pirates, coastal raiders, armies of undead, and evil wizards but how many have fought an epidemic, an idea, or an addiction?

The idea came from reading an article about the growing import market for flakka in the US of A.

While this may be less grand a quest than slaying a dragon or stopping an imperial navy from conquering your star system it seems more believable. Not all adventuring parties are composed of nobles, affluent merchants, or heirs to vast wealth. Many players choose to have a sorted upbringing. Therein lies the perfect story hook; the player's elderly relative was murdered during a robbery by an addict, another player's cousin was hung for murder after trying to get a fix, one of the party members was blackmailed with proof that their lover was an addict.

That being said the potion/drug/chemical should be a means to an end not the ultimate evil. I would recommend having some criminal mastermind, or manipulative agent, using the addiction to further their own goals. That being said the goals need not be self evident. Simply having the root cause being that criminals want to make money results in the party becoming a police force fighting a never ending battle.

  • A local warden is flooding the market with cheap chemicals to increase his commission on housing prisoners,
  • A brewer is using contacts to sell a devastating drug around competing bars in an effort to drive away business,
  • The local mining company has plans to buy land and is destroying the last neighborhood with addictions,
  • A foreign power has been losing money to get the country's troops dependent on a particular potion so they will be in withdrawal during the invasion.

It is roleplaying, adding some grey-area mortality is not a bad thing. In some ways the addicts are victims of circumstance, ignorance, or lies. The characters may be set up to deal with DPS, aggro, and spell allotments but there is no core rule book for dealing with emotional issues.
Idea - The enemy is an addictive potion/drug/chemical.
